overview:
Tiloyapannatti (often written Tiloya Pannatti; Sanskrit: Triloka-prajñaptiḥ) is a major early Jain Prakrit work devoted primarily to cosmography—the systematic description and measurement of the three worlds (triloka) that constitute the Jain universe. Composed in Jaina Śaurasenī Prakrit and largely in gāthā (āryā) metre, it belongs to the Karaṇānuyoga category of Jain literature, the ‘calculatory sciences’ concerned with cosmology, geography, astronomy, and quantitative description of reality. The text presents a highly structured account of the universe as beginningless, uncreated, and composed of six fundamental substances (dravya): jīva (living beings), pudgala (matter), dharma (medium of motion), adharma (medium of rest), kāla (time), and ākāśa (space). Within this framework, Tiloyapannatti maps the vertical and horizontal extent of the cosmos, the distribution of beings, and the pathways to liberation.

According to the author’s own enumeration, Tiloyapannatti is divided into nine Mahādhikāras (major sections), each further subdivided into adhikāras (subsections) and sometimes smaller units. These nine are: (1) the general nature of the universe (loka), (2) the hellish regions (naraka), (3) the mansion-dwelling deities (bhavanavāsī), (4) the human world (manuṣyaloka), (5) the sub-human world of plants, animals, and other non-human organisms (tiryag-loka), (6) the peripatetic or intermediate deities (vyantara), (7) the regions of light and luminaries (jyotiṣka), (8) the heavenly realms (devaloka), and (9) the realm of liberation (siddha-śilā). Across these nine sections the text comprises roughly 5,677 verses, with a small number of prose passages and occasional use of other metres such as Indravajrā, Upajāti, Dodhaka, Śārdūlavikrīḍita, Vasantatilakā, and Mālinī. This elaborate architecture allows the author to move from general cosmological principles to increasingly detailed descriptions of specific realms and their inhabitants.

Tiloyapannatti is especially notable for its quantitative precision. It defines and relates units of measurement—such as aṅgula (finger), hasta (hand), vitasti (span), daṇḍa (rod), kośa (distance measure), and rajju (a very large unit)—and uses them to calculate the dimensions of continents, oceans, mountains, and cosmic regions. It also discusses vast temporal units like sāgaropama and ardha-pāla, integrating them into a broader scheme of cosmic cycles and durations. In doing so, the text aligns with and sometimes anticipates other Jain cosmological treatises such as Sūrya-prajñapti, Candra-prajñapti, and Jambūdvīpa-prajñapti, while maintaining its own distinctive structure and terminology.

Authorship is traditionally attributed to Ācārya Yativṛṣabha (also referred to as Jadi-vasaha), an early Digambara scholar. Internal verses near the end of the ninth Mahādhikāra are interpreted as alluding to his name through śleṣa (wordplay), and external testimonies—such as Indranandi’s Śrutāvatāra and the Jayadhavalā commentary on Kaṣāya-prahṛta—associate Yativṛṣabha with other learned works and identify him as a disciple of Ārya Maṅkṣu and a close pupil of Nāgāhasti. On the basis of linguistic features, intertextual references, and historical notices (including a chronology of ruling dynasties after Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa), modern scholarship tentatively places Yativṛṣabha and Tiloyapannatti between the late 5th and early 7th centuries CE, after authors like Kundakunda and Sarvanandi and before figures such as Vīrasena and Jinabhadra Kṣamāśramaṇa.

Beyond cosmography, Tiloyapannatti offers valuable glimpses into Jain dogmatics, ritual culture, and intellectual history. The opening portions include invocations to the Pañca-parameṣṭhi (the five supreme beings) and a nuanced discussion of maṅgala (auspiciousness), its etymology, types (name, establishment, place, time, disposition), and the rationale for beginning a literary work with auspicious remembrance. Throughout the text, doctrinal elements—such as the classification of beings, the nature of karmic bondage, and the conditions for liberation—are woven into cosmological exposition. The final Mahādhikāra on the siddha-śilā (abode of liberated souls) connects the spatial description of the highest realm with the ethical and spiritual path leading to it, thereby integrating cosmology with soteriology.

Textually, Tiloyapannatti survives in a limited manuscript tradition, and modern editors have noted corrupt readings, missing lines, numerical inconsistencies, and occasional gaps in section titles. These issues suggest both the antiquity of the work and the challenges of transmission. The author himself sometimes acknowledges that certain traditional data were not available or had been lost, indicating a critical awareness of his sources. Despite these textual difficulties, the work is regarded within the tradition as an authentic and foundational presentation of Jain cosmology, and it continues to inform later diagrams, temple art, and pedagogical materials that depict the three worlds and the path of the soul within them.

primary_sources.title: Tiloyapannatti (Triloka-prajñaptiḥ)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Yativṛṣabha (Jadi-vasaha)
primary_sources.translation: Tiloyapannatti, composed in Jaina Śaurasenī Prakrit, systematically expounds the three worlds of Jain cosmology. It begins with invocations to the Pañca-parameṣṭhi and a definition of auspiciousness (maṅgala), then proceeds to describe the loka (universe) as beginningless and uncreated, constituted by six substances (dravya). Across nine major sections it details the hellish regions, mansion-dwelling deities, human and sub-human worlds, intermediate deities, luminaries, heavenly realms, and the realm of liberated souls. The text defines precise units of space and time, calculates the dimensions of continents, oceans, and cosmic regions, and situates all categories of beings within this structured universe, culminating in the description of the siddha-śilā where liberated souls abide.
primary_sources.notes: Primary Prakrit cosmological treatise classified under Karaṇānuyoga. The work is largely in gāthā metre, with occasional use of other metres and prose. Modern critical editions (e.g., those edited by A. N. Upadhye, Hiralal Jain, and others) rely on a small number of manuscripts and note corrupt readings and lacunae. Internal and external evidence support attribution to Yativṛṣabha and a date between the late 5th and early 7th centuries CE.

primary_sources.title: Introduction to Tiloyapannatti
primary_sources.author: A. N. Upadhye (editor and commentator)
primary_sources.translation: The scholarly introduction to Tiloyapannatti outlines the structure of the text into nine Mahādhikāras, describes the metres and prose passages employed, and discusses the manuscript basis of the edition. It analyzes internal verses that hint at the author’s identity, correlates them with external testimonies from works like Śrutāvatāra and Jayadhavalā, and proposes a historical placement for Yativṛṣabha. The introduction also highlights the text’s role within Karaṇānuyoga literature and comments on its linguistic features, noting the vitality of Prakrit and the author’s stylistic choices.
primary_sources.notes: While not itself a primary canonical text, this introduction is a key Tier B/C resource for understanding Tiloyapannatti’s structure, authorship, and transmission. It distinguishes between the cosmological core of the work and later interpretive layers, and it documents textual issues such as corrupt readings and missing subsections.

misconceptions.myth: Tiloyapannatti is only a mythological or symbolic text with no internal structure or technical precision.
misconceptions.reality: Tiloyapannatti is a highly structured and technically detailed cosmological treatise. It is divided into nine major sections, each with subsections, and it carefully defines units of space and time to calculate the dimensions of cosmic regions. Its descriptions are systematic and quantitative, reflecting the Karaṇānuyoga emphasis on calculatory sciences rather than mere narrative myth.

misconceptions.myth: Tiloyapannatti is a sectarian Śvetāmbara scripture and does not belong to the Digambara tradition.
misconceptions.reality: Tiloyapannatti is generally associated with the Digambara tradition and with the early Digambara scholar Ācārya Yativṛṣabha. Its language, intertextual references, and reception history place it within the broader Digambara cosmological and doctrinal corpus, even though its cosmological content is of interest across Jain sects.

misconceptions.myth: Because modern cosmology differs from Jain cosmology, Tiloyapannatti is obsolete and has no contemporary relevance.
misconceptions.reality: Tiloyapannatti does not aim to compete with modern physical cosmology; instead, it presents a religious-philosophical map of the universe that integrates ethics, soteriology, and metaphysics. Its value today lies in illuminating Jain conceptions of space, time, and the soul’s journey, in preserving historical units of measurement and cosmological diagrams, and in providing context for Jain art, ritual, and doctrinal discussions about the structure of reality and the path to liberation.

misconceptions.myth: Tiloyapannatti is a purely cosmological text and does not address doctrine, ritual, or culture.
misconceptions.reality: While cosmography is its primary focus, Tiloyapannatti also touches on Jain dogmatics, ritual invocations, and cultural-historical material. The opening discussion of maṅgala, the invocations to the Pañca-parameṣṭhi, and scattered references to ethical and soteriological themes show that the text integrates doctrinal and cultural concerns into its cosmological framework.
